section_1.title: Prerequisite Review: The First Derivative
section_1.content: Recall that the first derivative f'(x) represents the instantaneous rate of change (slope of the tangent line). Visually, if f(x) is position, f'(x) is velocity.
section_1.example: A cheetah chasing prey: f(x) is the distance covered, f'(x) is how fast the cheetah is moving at a specific moment.

section_2.title: Defining Higher Order Derivatives
section_2.content: A higher order derivative is simply the derivative of a derivative. If f'(x) is a function, we can differentiate it again to get f''(x) (the second derivative). Graphically, this represents the rate at which the slope itself is changing (concavity).
section_2.example: Visual animation: A graph showing a tangent line; as x moves, the slope of the tangent line changes. The second derivative tracks how quickly that slope is tilting.

section_3.title: Physical Interpretation: Acceleration
section_3.content: Bridge the concept to physics. If f'(x) is velocity, then f''(x) is acceleration. If the velocity is increasing, the second derivative is positive. If decreasing, it is negative.
section_3.example: A rocket launch: The position is f(t), velocity is f'(t), and the G-force felt by the pilot corresponds to the second derivative, f''(t).

section_4.title: Computational Step-by-Step
section_4.content: Demonstrate the power rule application. Differentiate f(x) = x^4, then f'(x) = 4x^3, then f''(x) = 12x^2, and f'''(x) = 24x.
section_4.example: An animation of a 'Derivative Machine' taking an input function and stripping away power layers one by one to reveal the 'DNA' of the curve's growth.

section_5.title: Summary and Intuition
section_5.content: Higher-order derivatives quantify how 'curvy' or volatile a function is. They are essential for optimization and modeling complex natural phenomena.
section_5.example: Closing visual: A roller coaster track. The height is f(x), the steepness is f'(x), and the 'jerk' or feeling of change in force is f''(x).

        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
